title: Binary tree basics: structure, terminology, and recursive contracts
summary: Treat each node as the entry to a subtree, and define height, depth, and return values before writing recursion.

sections.heading: Meaning and boundaries
paragraphs: Each node in a binary tree has at most two children, and left and right are distinct positions. An empty tree is valid input; a leaf has no left or right child. This chapter measures height in nodes: an empty tree has height zero and a single-node tree has height one. Node depth starts at one at the root. Sources that count edges differ by one, so agree on the convention before coding.

sections.heading: Core idea and invariant
paragraphs: A node object stores a value and two references; equal values do not make two nodes the same object. Linked storage suits ordinary sparse trees. Heaps often use arrays, but their index formulas cannot be applied indiscriminately to arbitrary compact level-order input. Let n denote the number of nodes, h the height, and w the maximum level width. These three quantities determine the space used by different algorithms.

sections.heading: Derivation and correctness
paragraphs: Think of recursion as a contract for a subtree: given its entry node, return specified information. The example returns both node count and height. An empty subtree returns zeros; a parent adds the two counts plus one, and takes the larger height plus one. If the child results are correct, both combination rules are correct, giving a structural induction proof for the whole algorithm.

Consider both extremes of tree shape: a seven-node chain has height seven and width one; a perfect seven-node tree has height three and maximum width four. The former is more likely to exhaust the recursion stack, while the latter keeps more nodes in a queue. Equal node counts do not imply equal memory use for a traversal.

sections.heading: Python implementation and adaptations
paragraphs: TreeNode instances are mutable Python objects. Assigning root to another variable copies only a reference, not the whole tree. Recursion depth equals the current path length; an extreme chain can exceed the interpreter recursion limit and can be handled with an explicit stack. The test constructor accepts a level-order array, where None marks a missing position rather than an ordinary node value.

time: O(n), where n is the node count; each node combines results once.
space: O(h), where h is the tree height; the returned pair has constant size.

The root combines them into (4,3).

An ordinary binary tree can have height n.

title: Recursive preorder traversal
summary: Fix where the current node is processed to obtain root, left, right order.

sections.heading: Meaning and boundaries
paragraphs: The input is any binary tree, and the output is a list of node values in root, left, right order. Every actual node appears exactly once; null references are excluded. Equal values may appear repeatedly because traversal visits nodes rather than deduplicated values. An empty tree returns an empty list without needing a dummy root.

sections.heading: Core idea and invariant
paragraphs: The contract of visit is to append the traversal of the entire current subtree to the same answer list. The parent is output before its children, making this useful for recording structure as it unfolds from the root. Neither subtree is complete when the current node is processed, so this position is unsuitable for depending on child statistics. A shared result list avoids creating and concatenating sublists at every level; repeated copying on a chain could otherwise turn a linear algorithm into a quadratic one.

sections.heading: Derivation and correctness
paragraphs: Start with the empty tree: the function returns immediately, as there are no nodes to visit. For a nonempty tree, assume the recursive calls correctly traverse the left and right subtrees. Placing the current value at the prescribed position then gives the correct order for this tree. Do not reverse the child calls, because left and right positions are part of the binary tree structure.

Preorder is often used for serialization, but values alone cannot uniquely reconstruct an ordinary tree: root 1 with left child 2 and root 1 with right child 2 both produce [1,2]. Record null-child markers to preserve structure. This also explains why construction problems need inorder as an additional source of structural information.

sections.heading: Python implementation and adaptations
paragraphs: An inner function encapsulates recursion, so the result list is created only once per solve call. Consecutive calls on different trees therefore do not reuse earlier results or require a global variable. append mutates a list in place, so the inner function can use the outer list directly; rebinding answer instead requires an understanding of scope rules. Convert recursion to an explicit stack for very deep trees.

time: O(n); each node is visited once.
space: O(h) recursion stack, plus an O(n) output list.

walkthrough: Begin recursion at root 1.

The final output is [1,2,4,3].

pitfalls: The position of value processing determines preorder, inorder, or postorder.
Return immediately for a null reference; do not read its val.
Do not put the result list in a default argument shared across calls.

title: Recursive postorder traversal
summary: Fix where the current node is processed to obtain left, right, root order.

sections.heading: Meaning and boundaries
paragraphs: The input is any binary tree, and the output is a list of node values in left, right, root order. Every actual node appears exactly once; null references are excluded. Equal values may appear repeatedly because traversal visits nodes rather than deduplicated values. An empty tree returns an empty list without needing a dummy root.

sections.heading: Core idea and invariant
paragraphs: The contract of visit is to append the traversal of the entire current subtree to the same answer list. Children are output before their parent, making this useful for height, balance, deletion, and other tasks needing subtree information first. Postorder describes when a value is processed, not when the function is first called. A shared result list avoids creating and concatenating sublists at every level; repeated copying on a chain could otherwise turn a linear algorithm into a quadratic one.

If processing means deleting the current node, postorder ensures that children are handled first. If it means computing height, both recursive calls must return heights for the root to combine. title: Iterative traversal: simulate calls with an explicit stack
summary: Preorder controls pop order, inorder records where to return, and postorder uses reversal to put children before parents.

sections.heading: Meaning and boundaries
paragraphs: Recursion and iteration visit the same nodes; they differ in where unfinished work is stored. Preorder can push nodes awaiting visits directly. Inorder must retain ancestors while descending a left chain. Postorder must also ensure both subtrees are output before their parent. The example provides three independent functions for cross-checking the same tree.

sections.heading: Core idea and invariant
paragraphs: A stack is last in, first out. Preorder visits the left subtree first, so push the right child before the left. Inorder maintains this invariant: the left side of each stacked node is being visited or has been visited, but the node itself has not been output. Push the whole left chain; after popping and outputting a node, enter its right subtree. Each node is pushed and popped once.

sections.heading: Derivation and correctness
paragraphs: For postorder, first obtain root, right, left order, then reverse it to get left, right, root. Push the left child first so the right child pops first. This reversal method stores all visited values. If processing means deleting nodes or computing subtree information, reversing a value list at the end is insufficient; use markers or explicit state instead.

Check stack templates with a single node and one-sided chains. A left chain 1→2→3 has preorder [1,2,3] and both inorder and postorder [3,2,1]; for a right chain, inorder equals preorder. These chains reveal left/right scheduling errors, but a branching tree is also needed to distinguish postorder child order. Chains alone cannot establish correctness.

sections.heading: Python implementation and adaptations
paragraphs: Python list append and pop work well as stack operations. Do not use pop(0), which shifts later elements. The outer inorder loop must test node or stack, because ancestors may still await processing when the current pointer is null. The code separates result collection from node scheduling to make differences among the three templates easy to compare.

time: All three traversals take O(n) time.
space: Preorder and inorder use an O(h) auxiliary stack; reversed postorder uses O(n) temporary results. All output lists take O(n).

walkthrough: At the root, preorder pushes 3 before 2.

pitfalls: Push order is the reverse of pop order.

title: Unified iteration: distinguish expansion from processing with state
summary: Separate node expansion and result output into two frame states to implement all three traversals in one framework.

sections.heading: Meaning and boundaries
paragraphs: Ordinary iterative templates differ in when they process the current node. A unified template adds a Boolean state to each stack element: False means expand the subtree, while True means output the current value immediately. An empty tree has no expansion tasks and returns an empty result. The order parameter selects pre, in, or post; invalid values explicitly raise an exception.

sections.heading: Core idea and invariant
paragraphs: When expanding a node, first list actions in their desired logical order, then push them in reverse. Preorder actions are process root, expand left, expand right; inorder actions are expand left, process root, expand right; postorder actions are expand left, expand right, process root. A node marked True is never expanded again, preventing an infinite loop.

sections.heading: Derivation and correctness
paragraphs: Each node produces one processing frame and at most two child-expansion frames. The stack top is always the next action to execute, simulating suspension and resumption of recursive calls. For inorder, the root processing frame sits below the left subtree task, so the entire left subtree finishes before the root is processed. The right task runs afterward.

Consider postorder for root 1 with left child 2. The stack initially holds the root expansion task. Expansion leaves its processing task at the bottom, so the left subtree runs first. That subtree creates its own processing task and outputs 2; only then does the root processing task pop and output 1. Different stages of the same node may coexist on the stack, but expansion happens only once.

sections.heading: Python implementation and adaptations
paragraphs: A Boolean in a tuple is clearer than a None marker and cannot be confused with a missing child. Only actual children receive tasks, avoiding empty stack work. The True phase can also be replaced with subtree-statistics processing, but child return values then need additional storage. Listing logical actions before pushing them is more reliable than memorizing three push-order recipes.

time: O(n); each node is expanded and processed once.

walkthrough: Expand the root into a left task, root processing, and a right task.
Reverse pushing makes the left task pop first.
Left, root, and right produce 2, 1, and 3.

pitfalls: Logical action order is not the direct push order.
A node with ready=True must not be expanded again.
Postorder must schedule the processing frame after both children.

title: Level-order traversal and per-level statistics
summary: Freeze the queue length at each level boundary to separate next-level children from current-level output.

sections.heading: Meaning and boundaries
paragraphs: Level-order traversal visits nodes by distance from the root and returns a two-dimensional list grouped by level. The root occupies the first level alone; nodes within a level appear left to right. An empty tree returns an empty list. Unlike depth-first traversal, level order naturally preserves horizontal boundaries, supporting rightmost values, averages, maxima, and bottom-up level-order results.

sections.heading: Core idea and invariant
paragraphs: A queue is first in, first out. At the start of each round, it contains exactly the nodes of the current level. Record size, pop exactly that many nodes, and append their children at the back. Although queue length changes, the number of pops in this round remains fixed. Children are processed only in the next round and never mix into the current level.

sections.heading: Derivation and correctness
paragraphs: Enqueuing the root establishes the first-level invariant. Adding each current node's left child before its right child orders the next level left to right as well. After the fixed number of pops, no current-level nodes remain, and the queue contains only the next level. Induction gives every level correctly. Each node enters and leaves the queue once, without a visited set.

Consider a root with two children: the left child has two children, while the right has none. The second round begins with size=2. After processing the left child, the queue temporarily contains the right child and two grandchildren, a length of three, but only one more parent-level node should be processed this round. This shows why changing queue length cannot replace a frozen level boundary.

sections.heading: Python implementation and adaptations
paragraphs: In Python, use collections.deque.popleft rather than repeated list pop(0). Problem 107 reverses the list of levels; 199 takes the last value of each level; 637 computes averages; 515 takes maxima. All use the same grouped result. The code demonstrates these applications, but when only statistics are needed in production, accumulate them directly per level to avoid storing the full two-dimensional result.

time: O(n); the combined work of the four statistical applications is also O(n).
space: O(w) queue, where w is maximum level width; grouped results and application outputs total O(n).

walkthrough: The queue begins as [3]; freeze its length at 1.
After outputting [3], the queue is [9,20].
The second round pops only two nodes; 15 and 7 wait for the third round.

pitfalls: Do not use while queue to consume every level as a single level.
Use / for averages, not integer division.
Reversing the level list does not reverse node order within each level.

title: N-ary tree level-order traversal
summary: Replace fixed left and right children with a children list; the proof of level boundaries stays the same.

sections.heading: Meaning and boundaries
paragraphs: An N-ary tree allows any number of children, with left-to-right order defined by their list. Input is a root object rather than the binary TreeNode; a null root still returns an empty list. Do not interpret N-ary serialized arrays with a binary-tree constructor, because grouping markers have different meanings.

sections.heading: Core idea and invariant
paragraphs: The queue stores nodes, not values. Freeze the node count at each level, output them in order, and append each node's children at the back. Every child belongs to the next level, so there is no need to recalculate depth inside children. Each parent-child edge causes exactly one enqueue.

sections.heading: Derivation and correctness
paragraphs: The first round contains only the root. Assuming the current queue follows within-level order, expanding children in that order collects children of leftward parents before those of rightward parents. The next level is therefore ordered correctly. Each nonroot tree node has exactly one parent, so no node is enqueued twice and no visited set is needed.

If the root has five children and only the last has children, the second round must still process all five before entering the grandchildren level. Empty children lists produce no placeholders; output includes actual nodes only. If several parents can reference the same object, the input no longer satisfies tree assumptions, and repeated graph visits need separate consideration.

sections.heading: Python implementation and adaptations
paragraphs: The example defines a separate Node class and creates a fresh list inside the constructor when children is None. Avoid children=[] as a default argument, which can make nodes share a mutable list. Space still depends on maximum level width: even a shallow tree with many children can require a linear-size queue.

time: O(n), where n is the number of N-ary tree nodes.

example.input: Root 1 has children 2 and 3; node 3 has child 4
walkthrough: Output root 1 first.
Enqueue children 2 and 3 in list order.
Node 3 adds 4 to the third level.

pitfalls: N-ary children are not equivalent to binary left and right children.
Avoid shared default lists.

title: Populate same-level next pointers
summary: Use the connected current level and a dummy head to link the next level; this also covers the perfect tree in problem 116.

sections.heading: Meaning and boundaries
paragraphs: Give each node a next pointer to its nearest neighbor on the right at the same level, or None at the level end. Problem 117 permits missing children; the perfect tree in 116 is a special case. Return the original root object, modifying nodes themselves. The algorithm assumes an ordinary tree whose left/right structure stays unchanged.

sections.heading: Core idea and invariant
paragraphs: Once the current level has a next chain, traverse it without a queue. Use dummy as the next chain's dummy head and tail as its last linked child. Scan current-level nodes left to right, checking their left and right children; append each actual child after tail. Parent order together with left/right child order guarantees next-level order.

sections.heading: Derivation and correctness
paragraphs: Set the root's next to None to establish the first-level chain. Each round starts at the current head and links all children into the next level. Finally set tail.next to None to clear any stale pointer. dummy.next is the next starting point; if there are no children, it is null and iteration ends. Each node is linked from its parent level once and scanned in its own level once.

sections.heading: Python implementation and adaptations
paragraphs: Do not assume node.left.next must point to node.right: an ordinary tree can lack either child, and links may need to cross several childless parents. A dummy head avoids special handling of the next level's first node. Each round retains only a few references and a temporary node, so auxiliary space is constant rather than proportional to width.

time: O(n); each node is scanned once.
space: O(1) extra space, with no recursion or queue.

walkthrough: The root forms the first-level chain.
Its children form 2→3.
Scanning 2→3 links their children into 5→7.

pitfalls: Links join same-level nodes, not inorder successors.
Clear next at the end of each new level.
Perfect-tree formulas do not directly handle missing children.

title: Invert a binary tree
summary: Swap every node's children to mirror the whole tree.

sections.heading: Meaning and boundaries
paragraphs: Inversion changes node connections rather than simply reversing traversal output. Each original left subtree becomes the right subtree and vice versa, with each subtree also mirrored internally. An empty tree returns None; a single-node tree returns the same node. The example modifies in place, so callers observe changes through their original root reference.

sections.heading: Core idea and invariant
paragraphs: The recursive contract returns the root of the inverted current subtree. No new root object is needed: swap its two references, then recursively invert the swapped children. Swapping before recursion or after recursion both work, provided each original child is processed exactly once.

sections.heading: Derivation and correctness
paragraphs: Assuming both child subtrees are correctly inverted, exchanging their positions at the root satisfies the mirror definition. Empty subtrees remain empty, so missing children require no special complication. Mirroring is not sorting: values play no role. Inverting a search tree generally breaks its original directional ordering constraints.

Inverting twice restores the original structure, which provides an additional check, but this property alone is insufficient: doing nothing also satisfies it. Check left/right positions after one inversion as well. A root with only a left child must end up with only a right child, clearly showing that null references participate in the swap.

sections.heading: Python implementation and adaptations
paragraphs: Python multiple assignment evaluates both right-hand references before assigning, so left,right=right,left is safe. Overwriting left with right before reading the old left can lose the original left subtree. Returning root keeps the interface consistent; recursive return values can also be used to reconnect children.

time: O(n); one swap per node.
space: O(h) recursion stack; in-place modification creates no separate tree.

walkthrough: Swap 2 and 7 at the root.
Node 7 swaps 6 and 9; node 2 swaps 1 and 3.
Leaves undergo no substantive change.

pitfalls: Reversing a level-order array does not produce the correct mirror.
Sequential assignments can overwrite an original subtree reference.

title: Symmetric binary tree
summary: Compare outer and inner positions in pairs rather than judging each subtree's shape separately.

sections.heading: Meaning and boundaries
paragraphs: Symmetry means the whole tree matches its mirror about the vertical axis through the root, in both shape and corresponding values. The root's subtrees must mirror each other. Empty and single-root trees are symmetric. Matching value traversals in two directions may be insufficient, because missing-node positions also encode structure.

sections.heading: Core idea and invariant
paragraphs: Define mirror(a,b) for two entries: return true if both are null, false if exactly one is null. Otherwise compare values, then a.left with b.right and a.right with b.left. Pairing direction is essential: comparing two left children tests ordinary equality, not mirroring.

sections.heading: Derivation and correctness
paragraphs: The null cases cover every termination condition. For a nonempty pair, equal values match the roots, while mirrored outer and inner subtrees match all remaining structure. These three conditions together are exactly equivalent to the two trees being mirrors. Begin with root.left and root.right to avoid comparing the root with itself unnecessarily.

A minimal counterexample is [1,2,2,None,3,None,3]: both 3 nodes are right children of their parents. Value counts match perfectly, but the tree is not symmetric. Outer pairing compares the left side's missing left child with the right side's actual right child and fails. Retaining null positions is more reliable than filtering them out before comparing values.

sections.heading: Python implementation and adaptations
paragraphs: Python and short-circuits: unequal values skip subtree comparisons, and a failed outer comparison can skip the inner one. Although each recursive call carries two nodes, maximum nesting still depends on tree height. There is no need to copy or physically invert the tree before comparison, which would use extra storage and could change the input.

time: O(n); all nodes may be examined.

walkthrough: Compare the two 2 nodes.
The outer 3 nodes match.
The inner 4 nodes match, as do both pairs of null children.

pitfalls: Comparison directions must cross.
Equal values with different null positions are still asymmetric.

title: Maximum depth of a binary tree
summary: Define the current subtree's height as the greater child height plus one.

sections.heading: Meaning and boundaries
paragraphs: Maximum depth is the number of nodes on the path from the root to its farthest leaf. An empty tree has depth zero; a childless root has depth one. Do not confuse depth with total node count: five nodes can form a chain of depth five or a branching tree of depth three. Return an integer; the deepest path itself need not be retained.

sections.heading: Core idea and invariant
paragraphs: Recursion returns subtree height rather than current depth accumulated from the root. Each child supplies its relative height, and the parent combines them with max(left,right)+1. The terms are related: a node's depth describes its position from the top, while its subtree height is a bottom-up statistic. At the root, both approaches give the same maximum.

sections.heading: Derivation and correctness
paragraphs: Any root-to-leaf path must first enter the left or right subtree. The longest path comes from the taller subtree, so taking the maximum is necessary and sufficient. Empty height zero automatically gives leaves max(0,0)+1=1, without a separate leaf case. Postorder structure makes child heights available before combination.

Equal left and right heights do not imply equal structures. Only path length matters here, so a maximum suffices. If the task instead asks for the deepest path, an integer alone does not identify a route; preserve a path or decide which side wins ties. Avoid burdening this implementation with information the task does not require.

sections.heading: Python implementation and adaptations
paragraphs: Python can place both recursive calls directly in return, but must handle a null root before reading children. A chain also makes the recursion stack linear. For very tall input, count BFS levels or use an explicit stack carrying node depths. A small average height does not justify claiming logarithmic worst-case space.

time: O(n); each node is computed once.
space: O(h), or O(n) for a worst-case chain.

walkthrough: Leaves 9, 15, and 7 have height 1.
Node 20 has height 2.
The root has height max(1,2)+1=3.

pitfalls: An empty tree has depth zero, not one.
Worst-case height is not O(log n).

title: Minimum depth of a binary tree
summary: Use breadth-first search to find the first actual leaf and avoid treating a missing subtree as a zero-length path.

sections.heading: Meaning and boundaries
paragraphs: Minimum depth is the number of nodes from the root to the nearest leaf. A leaf must lack both children. A root with only a right child is not a leaf, and its missing left subtree cannot count as a valid path of length zero. An empty tree returns zero and a single-node tree one. This definition prevents blindly reusing the maximum-depth formula.

sections.heading: Core idea and invariant
paragraphs: BFS visits nodes in increasing depth, so the first leaf encountered has minimum depth. Queue entries contain node and depth; each child has its parent's depth plus one. There is no need to inspect every leaf and then minimize, or to preserve paths when only length is requested.

sections.heading: Derivation and correctness
paragraphs: When a leaf at depth d is popped, every node at depth less than d has been processed. If any had been a leaf, the algorithm would already have stopped. Thus no shorter path is missed. Missing children never enter the queue: they affect leaf detection without creating false path candidates. This proof depends on every edge increasing depth by one.

For example, if the root's left child is a leaf and its right side extends ten levels, minimum depth is still two. BFS stops at the left leaf on level two without exploring the entire right chain. A recursive algorithm usually computes more descendants, demonstrating BFS's early-stop advantage on trees combining shallow leaves with deep branches.

sections.heading: Python implementation and adaptations
paragraphs: Use deque and carry depth in queue entries to avoid explicit level counting, while still checking that both children are null. A recursive version also works: with only one child, return that child's height plus one; take the minimum only when both children exist. BFS here expresses early stopping, though a wide tree can need more queue space than DFS stack space.

time: O(n) worst case; may stop early at the first shallow leaf.

walkthrough: Node 1 has a right child and is not a leaf.
Node 2 also has a right child.
Node 3 is the first leaf, at depth 3.

pitfalls: Do not directly calculate 1+min(left height,right height).
A node with one child is not a leaf.

title: Count nodes in a complete binary tree
summary: When leftmost and rightmost heights match, use the perfect-tree formula to skip an entire subtree.

sections.heading: Meaning and boundaries
paragraphs: Input is guaranteed to be a complete binary tree: every level except the last is full, and the last is filled continuously from the left. A perfect binary tree has every level full and is a special case. This guarantee is essential: equal boundary heights in an arbitrary tree do not rule out internal gaps.

sections.heading: Core idea and invariant
paragraphs: From the current root, follow left pointers and right pointers to obtain node-count heights a and b. In a complete tree, a==b means every level of this subtree is full, so return 2 to the power a minus one directly. Otherwise count both subtrees recursively and add the root.

sections.heading: Derivation and correctness
paragraphs: Incompleteness in a complete tree extends along only one path, so at each split at least one side quickly terminates through the perfect-tree formula. Recursion has O(log n) levels and measuring boundaries costs at most O(log n) per level, giving O(log² n) time. Counting every node is also correct but fails to exploit the structural guarantee.

The right subtree of a six-node complete tree is not full, so the seven-node perfect-tree formula cannot be applied at the root. Boundary measurement detects different heights and triggers a split. Perfect subproblems still use a constant-time power formula, but boundary measurement is not constant work. That is why complexity is squared logarithmic rather than logarithmic.

sections.heading: Python implementation and adaptations
paragraphs: The code uses (1 << a)-1 for the integer power, avoiding floating point. An empty tree has both heights zero and the formula would return zero, but an explicit empty case is clearer. Tests must use complete trees. Applying this template to an ordinary sparse tree can yield plausible but incorrect results.

time: O(log² n), valid only with the complete-tree guarantee.

walkthrough: The root has left boundary height 3 and right boundary height 2, so split.
The left subtree is perfect and contributes 3 directly.
The right subtree contributes 2; adding the root gives 6.

pitfalls: Equal boundary heights imply fullness only under the complete-tree guarantee.
The formula measures height in nodes.

title: Balanced binary tree
summary: Return heights in postorder, and propagate failure toward the root with a negative sentinel.

sections.heading: Meaning and boundaries
paragraphs: Height balance requires every node's child-subtree heights to differ by at most one, not just the root's. An empty tree is balanced. Equal heights at the root can hide imbalance deeper down, so every subtree must be checked. The final result is Boolean, but the helper must supply both height and failure status.

sections.heading: Core idea and invariant
paragraphs: Let height return a nonnegative height, or -1 for an unbalanced subtree. Obtain the left height first and propagate failure immediately; do the same for the right. If both are valid, check their difference: return -1 when it exceeds one, otherwise return the larger height plus one. Failure cannot be confused with valid empty height zero.

sections.heading: Derivation and correctness
paragraphs: This postorder combination computes each node's height once. Separately recomputing both heights at every node and then recursively checking balance repeatedly scans the same subtrees, taking O(n²) on a chain. The sentinel carries information in return values without a global variable. One failed subtree necessarily makes the whole tree fail.

Also test equal heights at the root with an internally unbalanced child. The current abs difference can be zero, yet the child failure still invalidates the whole tree. All valid heights are nonnegative, so -1 is unambiguous. If more statistics are needed, use a pair instead of numerical encoding.

sections.heading: Python implementation and adaptations
paragraphs: The top level checks whether the result equals -1; do not convert the height integer directly to bool, because an empty tree has height zero but should return True. Early returns are valid short-circuiting and skip no node that could alter the conclusion. Deep trees still use O(h) call-stack space, not constant auxiliary space.

time: O(n); each node is visited at most once.

walkthrough: Heights propagate upward from the 3 nodes.
The left subtree reaches height 3; the root's right subtree has height 1.
The difference at the root is 2, so return -1.

pitfalls: Check every node, not only the root.
Do not recompute whole subtree heights at each node.

title: All paths in a binary tree
summary: Use a shared list for the root-to-node route, create independent results at leaves, and undo each level's change on return.

sections.heading: Meaning and boundaries
paragraphs: Output every root-to-leaf path, joining values with arrows. Endpoints must be leaves; do not collect at internal nodes. An empty tree has no paths, while a single node has one path containing just its value. Child traversal order determines enumeration order, but the correctness of the path set does not depend on that order.

sections.heading: Core idea and invariant
paragraphs: Append the current value to path on entry, making path exactly the route from root to current node. At a leaf, convert the list into a stored string; otherwise recursively visit both children. On exit, pop to undo this append and restore the parent's state from before entering the child.

sections.heading: Derivation and correctness
paragraphs: Reusing one list across recursive branches is safe when entry and exit changes are strictly paired. Finishing the left branch restores path to the parent before the right branch starts, so the left leaf's value cannot leak across. join creates a new string, so later pops cannot change collected answers.

At each leaf, shared path length equals that path's depth. If many leaves share a long prefix, that prefix is repeated in every output string, and output size can greatly exceed node count. The algorithm cannot omit repeated text required by the task, so output length must be a complexity parameter.

sections.heading: Python implementation and adaptations
paragraphs: Convert node values to strings before join to support negatives and multiple digits. Storing path itself would make all results share one list, potentially leaving every answer empty at the end. Total path-string length can be quadratic, so include string construction in complexity rather than simply claiming O(n).

time: O(n+L), where L is total output-string length, including the digits of node values.
space: O(h) path and recursion stack; output takes O(L).

walkthrough: The path grows while entering 1, 2, and 5.
At leaf 5, save a string and backtrack to [1].
Enter 3 and save the second path.

pitfalls: Collect only at leaves.
Backtrack shared lists, and copy them when collecting list results.

title: Sum of left leaves
summary: A left leaf requires both a position and leaf status: inspect the left child, then search deeper subtrees recursively.

sections.heading: Meaning and boundaries
paragraphs: A left leaf is a parent's left child with no children of its own. A root has no parent, so even a childless root is not a left leaf. Values, level-order indices, and membership in the tree's left half do not determine this status. The sum can be negative; empty trees and trees without left leaves return zero.

sections.heading: Core idea and invariant
paragraphs: At each parent, check that left exists and both left.left and left.right are null. If so, add left.val as the local contribution. Then process both subtrees to find deeper left leaves. A parent contributes only its immediate left child, so descendants are not counted twice.

sections.heading: Derivation and correctness
paragraphs: Every nonroot node has one parent, so each left leaf is counted once when its parent is visited. An internal left child contributes nothing itself, but recursion can still discover left leaves beneath it. A right leaf never passes its parent's left check, and the root is never examined as anyone's child.

If the tree is a root with a left child that itself has a right child, the left child is not a leaf, and the deepest right child is not a left leaf. The answer is zero. This rules out two misconceptions: that all leaves inside a left subtree count, and that all left children should be added.

sections.heading: Python implementation and adaptations
paragraphs: Check that left exists first, using and short-circuiting before reading its children. Alternatively, carry an is_left flag recursively and decide contribution at leaves; both approaches encode position. Do not test truthiness of node values: a zero-valued leaf is still a valid node.

time: O(n).

walkthrough: Node 9 is the root's left leaf and contributes 9.
Node 15 is node 20's left leaf and contributes 15.
Node 7 is a right leaf and is excluded.

pitfalls: The root is not a left leaf.
A left child is not necessarily a leaf.

title: Find the bottom-left tree value
summary: Update the first node at every level; the final value is the leftmost on the deepest level.

sections.heading: Meaning and boundaries
paragraphs: Find the leftmost node on the deepest level, which need not be the leftmost leaf in the entire tree. The original problem guarantees a nonempty root. The example raises ValueError for an empty tree rather than using a valid integer as a no-result sentinel. Nodes within a level run left to right, so its first node is its leftmost.

sections.heading: Core idea and invariant
paragraphs: At each level-order round, the queue contains only current-level nodes. Read queue[0].val into answer, then pop the frozen number of nodes and enqueue their children left before right. Each deeper level overwrites the answer; when the queue empties, the stored value is the deepest level's first value.

sections.heading: Derivation and correctness
paragraphs: The first level contains only the root, so its first value is correct. Given a correctly ordered level, appending children in parent order and left before right establishes the next level's order. A round with no next level is the deepest, so the last update satisfies the task. An earlier shallow left leaf does not cause premature termination.

Suppose the root has a left leaf at depth two, while its right side has a left child at depth three. The answer lies in the root's right subtree because depth takes priority over horizontal position. Choosing a first value by level first identifies greatest depth, then the leftmost position there. The first left leaf encountered in the whole tree does not follow this priority.

sections.heading: Python implementation and adaptations
paragraphs: No per-level value list or stored depth is needed, only answer and the queue. Read the first node before emptying the current level. DFS also works: traverse left before right and update on first entering a greater depth, while correctly maintaining maximum depth and its comparison condition.

time: O(n).

walkthrough: First values of successive levels are 1, 2, 4, and 7.
The last level contains only 7.
Return the last recorded first value.

pitfalls: A shallower leftmost leaf may not be the answer.
Define empty-tree behavior explicitly.

title: Path sum
summary: Pass the target remainder after subtracting each value, and test for zero only at leaves.

sections.heading: Meaning and boundaries
paragraphs: Find a root-to-leaf path whose values sum to the target. It must include the root and end at a leaf; reaching the target at an internal node is not success. Values can be negative, so a negative remainder does not make completion impossible. An empty tree has no valid path and returns False even for target zero.

sections.heading: Core idea and invariant
paragraphs: The recursive contract asks whether the current subtree contains a complete path summing to remaining. Subtract the current value on entry. At a leaf, check whether the remainder is zero. At an internal node, either child can supply a path matching the remainder, so combine their results with or.

sections.heading: Derivation and correctness
paragraphs: Every descent subtracts exactly one node value. At a leaf, remaining equals the original target minus the complete path sum. Both recursive choices cover every possible next step, so no valid path is missed and no unfinished prefix is accepted. Null children fail directly, ensuring a missing branch is not a valid endpoint.

For root 1 with its only child -1 and target zero, the remainder at the root is -1, but the negative-valued leaf brings it back to zero, so the answer is success. Pruning requires reliable bounds on unseen values. Stopping when the current sum exceeds the target wrongly transfers an assumption from nonnegative arrays to general trees.

sections.heading: Python implementation and adaptations
paragraphs: remaining is an integer; passing a new value needs no manual undo and sibling calls cannot modify each other. or skips the right search after a valid left path is found, which suits existence queries. Collecting all paths instead requires exploring both sides and preserving the current route without this short-circuit structure.

time: O(n) worst case, with possible early exit when a path is found.

walkthrough: After 5, the remainder is 17.
After 4 and 11, it is 2.
Leaf 2 reduces it to zero; path 5→4→11→2 succeeds.

pitfalls: A zero remainder at an internal node is not immediate success.
Negative values prevent pruning by the sign of the remainder.

title: Path sum II
summary: Replace an existence search with exhaustive enumeration, copying the current path when a leaf matches the target.

sections.heading: Meaning and boundaries
paragraphs: Return all root-to-leaf paths summing to target, each represented as a value list. Unlike problem 112's Boolean result, finding the first answer does not end the search. An empty tree returns an empty list. Distinct node routes remain distinct tree paths even when their values match completely, and are normally retained separately in traversal order.

sections.heading: Core idea and invariant
paragraphs: path holds the root-to-current-node values; remaining is the sum still needed. Append and subtract on entry. At a leaf, check both the endpoint and remainder conditions, adding path.copy() on success. Pop on exit to restore the path for sibling branches.

sections.heading: Derivation and correctness
paragraphs: DFS visits every root-to-leaf path exactly once. Subtraction makes the sum test correct; copying prevents subsequent backtracking from changing the collected historical state. Undo the current node whether the leaf succeeds or fails. Returning directly on success without pop contaminates later answers.

Paths to two leaves can share a prefix, so their copied answers contain equal prefixes but must remain independent lists. After return, change one element of the first answer and confirm the second stays unchanged to test output ownership. Even for target zero, an empty tree has no path: an empty route is not a root-to-leaf path.

sections.heading: Python implementation and adaptations
paragraphs: Leaf testing comes before child recursion, so internal nodes are never collected. A mutable path keeps temporary space within tree height, but copying answers costs time proportional to total output length. Negative values still rule out remaining<0 pruning; optimization needs additional reliable subtree bounds rather than guesses based on the current remainder.

time: O(n+L), where L is the total number of nodes in output paths; worst case O(n²).
space: O(h) temporary path and recursion stack, plus O(L) output.

walkthrough: Left leaf 2 matches the remainder; copy the first path.
Backtrack to the root and explore the right subtree.
Right leaf 5 matches the remainder; copy the second path.

pitfalls: Store path.copy(), not the shared path.
Do not short-circuit when enumerating all answers.

title: Construct a binary tree from inorder and postorder
summary: Postorder's last value identifies the root; its inorder position splits subtrees, while indices avoid array copying.

sections.heading: Meaning and boundaries
paragraphs: Reconstruct a tree from its inorder and postorder sequences. Values are guaranteed distinct and both traversals valid, giving each value a unique inorder position. One traversal alone usually cannot determine the tree. Empty arrays represent an empty tree. The example parameter order is inorder, postorder.

sections.heading: Core idea and invariant
paragraphs: Inorder always lists left subtree, root, right subtree. Once the root index is known, [lo,mid) describes the left subtree and (mid,hi] the right. When consuming postorder backward, read root, then right subtree, then left subtree. Build right before left. Each consumption moves the cursor once.

sections.heading: Derivation and correctness
paragraphs: The builder reconstructs the subtree corresponding to the closed inorder interval lo..hi; lo>hi returns null. Consume a root value, locate its inorder index in a hash map, split the interval, and recursively attach children in consumption order. Valid input guarantees the root index lies in this interval. The two subintervals are disjoint and cover every remaining node, so each node is created exactly once.

For inorder [2,1,3] and postorder [2,3,1], backward consumption reads 1 and then 3, which belongs to the right interval. Recursing left first while consuming 3 places the root index outside that interval. This is not merely swapping children: the cursor and interval being built have lost their correspondence.

sections.heading: Python implementation and adaptations
paragraphs: Build an inorder position dictionary up front to avoid linear searches at every level. Pass index boundaries rather than slices, avoiding repeated copying on degenerate trees. The cursor lives in a closure and needs nonlocal when modified; the dictionary is read only and needs no such declaration. Duplicate values or invalid traversals require a newly defined ambiguity or validation policy. This template is not a general-purpose parser.

time: O(n); dictionary lookup is O(1) on average, and each node is built once.
space: O(n) index dictionary and O(h) stack, plus O(n) new tree.

walkthrough: Locate root 3, splitting inorder into [9] and [15,20,7].
Consume postorder backward and build right root 20 first.
Recursively split inorder intervals and attach both subtrees to the root.

pitfalls: Duplicate values make value-to-index mapping ambiguous.
Consumption order must match the traversal direction.
A slicing version can perform quadratic copying in the worst case.

title: Construct a binary tree from preorder and inorder
summary: Preorder's first value identifies the root; its inorder position splits subtrees, while indices avoid array copying.

sections.heading: Meaning and boundaries
paragraphs: Reconstruct a tree from its preorder and inorder sequences. Values are guaranteed distinct and both traversals valid, giving each value a unique inorder position. One traversal alone usually cannot determine the tree. Empty arrays represent an empty tree. The example parameter order is preorder, inorder.

sections.heading: Core idea and invariant
paragraphs: Inorder always lists left subtree, root, right subtree. Once the root index is known, [lo,mid) describes the left subtree and (mid,hi] the right. When consuming preorder forward, read root, then left subtree, then right subtree. Build left before right. Each consumption moves the cursor once.

sections.heading: Derivation and correctness
paragraphs: The builder reconstructs the subtree corresponding to the closed inorder interval lo..hi; lo>hi returns null. Consume a root value, locate its inorder index in a hash map, split the interval, and recursively attach children in consumption order. Valid input guarantees the root index lies in this interval. The two subintervals are disjoint and cover every remaining node, so each node is created exactly once.

For preorder [1,2,3] and inorder [2,1,3], consuming root 1 leaves 2 next, which belongs to the left interval. Building the right side first consumes 2 incorrectly, so the recursive order cannot be freely swapped. Each interval determines valid root positions, while the cursor identifies the next root; both must advance together.

sections.heading: Python implementation and adaptations
paragraphs: Build an inorder position dictionary up front to avoid linear searches at every level. Pass index boundaries rather than slices, avoiding repeated copying on degenerate trees. The cursor lives in a closure and needs nonlocal when modified; the dictionary is read only and needs no such declaration. Duplicate values or invalid traversals require a newly defined ambiguity or validation policy. This template is not a general-purpose parser.

time: O(n); dictionary lookup is O(1) on average, and each node is built once.
space: O(n) index dictionary and O(h) stack, plus O(n) new tree.

walkthrough: Locate root 3, splitting inorder into [9] and [15,20,7].
Consume preorder forward and build left leaf 9 first.
Recursively split inorder intervals and attach both subtrees to the root.

pitfalls: Duplicate values make value-to-index mapping ambiguous.
Consumption order must match the traversal direction.
A slicing version can perform quadratic copying in the worst case.

title: Maximum binary tree
summary: Maintain the right spine with a decreasing monotonic stack, attaching nodes displaced by a new maximum as its left subtree.

sections.heading: Meaning and boundaries
paragraphs: Array elements are distinct. A maximum binary tree uses an interval's maximum as root, recursively building the left subtree from elements before it and the right subtree from elements after it. Scanning for the maximum at every recursive level can take quadratic time on increasing or decreasing arrays. A monotonic stack builds the same structure online from left to right.

sections.heading: Core idea and invariant
paragraphs: The stack stores the rightmost path of the portion already built, with strictly decreasing values. When node arrives, pop every smaller stack top; the last popped subtree root becomes node.left. If the stack remains nonempty, its larger top takes node as its new right child. Push node to restore the decreasing spine.

sections.heading: Derivation and correctness
paragraphs: Popped nodes lie left of the new value and are smaller, so they belong to its left subtree. Popping moves from the smaller right end toward larger ancestors. The last popped node already contains the earlier structure, so attaching it as the left root preserves all existing children. The surviving top is the nearest still-larger ancestor on the left; attaching a right child preserves the array's inorder sequence.

Increasing [1,2,3] yields root 3 with left child 2 and left grandchild 1; a decreasing array yields a right chain. These are both worst cases for repeated maximum scans and useful stack checks. One incoming value can pop many nodes, but total pops never exceed the number of nodes created.

sections.heading: Python implementation and adaptations
paragraphs: Repeatedly assigning node.left inside while is intentional: the final assignment retains the last popped whole subtree. With no pops, the left child stays null; emptying the stack makes the new node the global root. Every node is pushed once and popped at most once, so nested loops still take linear time. Finally stack[0] is the root; an empty array returns None.

time: O(n); each node is pushed once and popped at most once.
space: O(n) monotonic stack, plus O(n) output tree.

walkthrough: 3, 2, and 1 form a decreasing right chain.
6 pops the entire spine and takes root 3 as its left child.
5 pops 0, becomes the right child of 6, and takes 0 as its own left child.

pitfalls: The last popped node is the left subtree entry.
Distinct elements are guaranteed; duplicates require an explicit root tie rule.

title: Merge two binary trees
summary: Recurse over two matching positions, add overlapping values, and copy one-sided positions into new nodes.

sections.heading: Meaning and boundaries
paragraphs: When both trees contain a node at the same position, add their values; when only one does, preserve that side's structure and value. The example creates a fully independent new tree so original inputs can be reused. Returning an existing one-sided subtree would satisfy the value and structure requirements but share nodes between the merged tree and its input.

sections.heading: Core idea and invariant
paragraphs: Recursive arguments represent the same position in both trees. Return null if both are null; otherwise create a node, treating the missing side's value as zero. Recursively merge corresponding children for left and right. Check each entry before reading its children; there is no need to materialize an empty tree as zero-valued nodes.

sections.heading: Derivation and correctness
paragraphs: The two input positions uniquely determine the merged value. Recursion preserves this pairing for child positions, establishing the result by induction. Even when only one side exists, recursion clones its descendants, ensuring every output node is new. A zero contribution is only an arithmetic convention, not a reason to treat an existing zero-valued node as absent.

With a single-node tree and an empty tree, the output value matches the input, but this implementation's root must be a different object. Level-order values alone cannot reveal shared references; check identity separately. Independent output can be modified without affecting inputs, at the cost of allocating nodes even at one-sided positions.

sections.heading: Python implementation and adaptations
paragraphs: The code uses conditional expressions to read children safely on null sides. A dedicated clone helper for an absent side can reduce branching. If an application permits sharing, returning that side directly reduces creation work, but explain the effect of later mutations. Complexity depends on both trees' total size, not just their overlap.

time: O(n₁+n₂), where n₁ and n₂ are the two node counts.
space: O(max(h₁,h₂)) stack, plus a new tree bounded by O(n₁+n₂).

walkthrough: The root becomes 1+2=3.
The left root becomes 3+1=4; the right becomes 2+3=5.
One-sided nodes 5, 4, and 7 are copied into corresponding positions.

pitfalls: Specify whether one-sided subtrees are shared.
A zero value is not a missing node.

title: Search in a binary search tree
summary: Use whole-subtree ordering constraints to choose just one direction at each step.

sections.heading: Meaning and boundaries
paragraphs: In a binary search tree, every left-subtree value is smaller than its root and every right-subtree value is larger. This section uses the strict definition with no duplicates. Search for a value and return its node object, the entry to the subtree rooted there; return None if absent. Do not return a newly created node containing only the target value.

sections.heading: Core idea and invariant
paragraphs: Compare target with the current val: return on equality, go left when smaller, and right when larger. Each step rules out an entire side, relying on the global search-tree property rather than merely direct-child comparisons. For an ordinary binary tree, a single-branch search could miss an existing node.

sections.heading: Derivation and correctness
paragraphs: The loop invariant states that if the target exists, it lies in the current subtree. Choosing by value preserves that possibility. A null entry means the candidate set is empty and search fails. Path length depends on height: balanced trees are faster, but a degenerate chain can require scanning every node.

A missing target between node values usually reaches a null child. Searching for 5 in [4,2,7,1,3] follows 4→7→null left child. Other branches need no inspection because ancestor comparisons already excluded them. Performance still depends on shape; an ordinary search tree does not automatically remain balanced.

sections.heading: Python implementation and adaptations
paragraphs: Iteration uses only one moving pointer and no recursion stack. return root returns the original reference, so modifying the returned node changes the original tree. Tests convert the returned subtree with values, verifying both the found value and the correct structural entry.

time: O(h): O(log n) for a balanced tree and O(n) for a degenerate tree.

walkthrough: 2 is less than 4, so go left.
The current value equals 2; stop.
Return the original node reference.

pitfalls: A search-tree guarantee is required.
Return a node, not a Boolean.

title: Validate a binary search tree
summary: Pass ancestor-defined open intervals downward to check every inherited constraint.

sections.heading: Meaning and boundaries
paragraphs: Determine whether an ordinary binary tree is a strict binary search tree; duplicates are forbidden. Checking only left child < parent and right child > parent is insufficient because deeper nodes also inherit ancestor restrictions. An empty tree is valid. For example, a 3 inside root 5's right subtree violates the global >5 rule even if it is less than its own parent 6.

sections.heading: Core idea and invariant
paragraphs: The recursive function carries lower and upper, the strict open interval allowed for the current node. The root has no bounds. Entering the left side tightens upper to the current value; entering the right tightens lower, while other ancestor bounds persist. Any value not strictly inside its interval immediately fails.

sections.heading: Derivation and correctness
paragraphs: The interval is the intersection of every comparison constraint along the root path. A valid current value and two valid child subtrees ensure all left values are smaller and all right values larger, while each internal node meets the same rule. Null children add no constraints and return true. Thus local recursion expresses the entire global property.

Equal adjacent inorder values must also fail strict validation. Bounds make any repeated ancestor value hit an open endpoint, not merely fail on direct parent equality. Very large and small integers can still be compared directly. None for an absent bound avoids excluding valid inputs beyond assumed fixed integer limits.

sections.heading: Python implementation and adaptations
paragraphs: None denotes no bound, avoiding assumptions about integer ranges and unnecessary floating sentinels. Use <= and >= to reject equality. Strictly increasing inorder is an equivalent validation approach, useful alongside minimum-difference and mode templates; interval checking expresses ancestor constraints more directly.

time: O(n); all nodes may need validation.

walkthrough: Root 5 is valid.
Right node 6 receives lower bound 5.
Node 3 inherits lower bound 5 and fails.

pitfalls: Valid direct children do not guarantee a valid whole tree.
Strict search trees must reject duplicates.

title: Minimum absolute difference in a binary search tree
summary: Compare adjacent inorder values rather than every pair of nodes.

sections.heading: Meaning and boundaries
paragraphs: The tree is guaranteed to have at least two nodes; find the minimum absolute difference between distinct nodes' values. Inorder is nondecreasing or strictly increasing depending on whether duplicates are allowed. Even with duplicates, this algorithm correctly obtains zero. The example raises ValueError for fewer than two nodes, so the interface always returns a definite finite difference.

sections.heading: Core idea and invariant
paragraphs: In a sorted sequence, any nonadjacent pair has intervening values, and its difference cannot be smaller than every adjacent difference between them. Thus an adjacent pair achieves the minimum. Inorder needs only previous and the best difference, without constructing the whole sequence or sorting all values.

sections.heading: Derivation and correctness
paragraphs: An explicit stack descends left chains; each popped node supplies the next sorted value. If previous exists, update the minimum using current value minus previous, then set previous to the current value. The first node has no predecessor and must skip subtraction. Each later adjacent pair is examined exactly once.

Even a two-node tree requires one difference check. Root 0 with left child -3 has inorder [-3,0] and answer 3. If duplicate node values are allowed, adjacent duplicates produce zero without breaking the algorithm. This returns a numeric difference; returning the corresponding node pair would also require the predecessor object reference.

sections.heading: Python implementation and adaptations
paragraphs: Do not initialize previous to zero: negative values are possible and zero is valid. None marks uninitialized state without assumptions about the value range. The answer also starts as None and receives the first difference directly. Without the search-tree guarantee, inorder may be unsorted and current minus previous may be negative, invalidating this proof.

time: O(n).

walkthrough: Inorder is 1, 2, 3, 4, 6.
Adjacent differences are 1, 1, 1, 2.
The minimum difference is 1.

pitfalls: At least two nodes are required.
Predecessor initialization must not reserve a valid numeric value.

title: Find modes in a binary search tree
summary: Inorder groups equal values into runs; use run counts to track maximum frequency and tied answers.

sections.heading: Meaning and boundaries
paragraphs: This search tree permits duplicates: left-subtree values are at most the root and right-subtree values at least the root. Modes are the most frequent values, and there can be several. An empty tree returns an empty list. An ordinary binary tree can use a frequency dictionary, but sorted inorder groups equal values contiguously and avoids a table keyed by every distinct value.

sections.heading: Core idea and invariant
paragraphs: Maintain previous, current run length count, maximum frequency best, and an answer list. Equal current and previous values increment count; a changed value begins a new run with count one. When count exceeds best, all earlier answers become invalid, so replace them with the current value. When count equals best, append the current value.

sections.heading: Derivation and correctness
paragraphs: Comparing counts before a run ends is still correct. Each increment can set a new maximum, and replacing the list then removes earlier temporary candidates. A tie appends once; further growth in the same run sets a new maximum and replaces the list, preventing duplicate answers from persisting. Ultimately each value's complete frequency determines its membership.

Trace sorted visits [1,1,2,2]: the first 1 establishes frequency one, the second raises it to two. The first 2 has not reached two; the second 2 is appended as a tied mode. Thus a new value should not immediately join the answer when a run changes, and updates need not wait until the run ends.

sections.heading: Python implementation and adaptations
paragraphs: Initialize best=0 and previous=None so the first actual value begins the first run correctly. Node values are integers, so None cannot collide with a valid value. Iterative inorder uses O(h) stack space. Output may contain every distinct value, so its space is not constant. Morris traversal can reduce stack use further, at the cost of temporarily changing pointers.

time: O(n).
space: O(h) stack, plus O(k) output for k modes.

walkthrough: Inorder is 1, 2, 2.
1 and the first 2 temporarily both have frequency 1.
The second 2 raises the maximum to 2, replacing the answer with [2].

pitfalls: A new maximum must discard all old candidates.
Duplicate rules differ from the strict validation in problem 98.

title: Lowest common ancestor in a binary tree
summary: Report target locations upward in postorder; hits on both sides identify the branching node.

sections.heading: Meaning and boundaries
paragraphs: Given an ordinary binary tree and two actual nodes p and q, find the lowest ancestor containing both. A node counts as its own ancestor, so if p is an ancestor of q, the answer is p. As in the original problem, assume both targets exist and are distinct. Compare node identity, not value. Distinct values in the example do not change that interface.

sections.heading: Core idea and invariant
paragraphs: Return None for a null entry, or the node itself when it is p or q. Search both subtrees. Two nonnull results place the targets on opposite sides, making the current node their common ancestor. With only one nonnull side, propagate that result. A return value can represent either one target or an already determined common ancestor.

sections.heading: Derivation and correctness
paragraphs: When targets lie on opposite sides, no strict descendant of the current node can cover both, so it is the lowest ancestor. If one target is an ancestor of the other, returning it immediately is valid because it already covers the other target's subtree. This relies on both targets existing; otherwise verify existence separately or return a target count.

If a result is already a common ancestor, the opposite side cannot contain another target, as that would contradict the earlier placement of both targets. Under the existence guarantee, one node reference therefore represents several states. With a missing target, a lone target reference could be mistaken for the final answer, making the contract essential.

sections.heading: Python implementation and adaptations
paragraphs: Use is for object identity rather than comparing node.val. Tests obtain p and q references directly from the constructed tree. The function uses no search-tree ordering, so arbitrary shapes are supported. A degenerate tree creates deep recursion. If recursion is unsuitable, build a parent-pointer map and intersect ancestor chains, using more space.

time: O(n); the whole tree may be scanned.

walkthrough: Return the reference immediately on reaching node 5.
The root's right side contains no target and returns None.
The root propagates left result 5.

pitfalls: The interface assumes both targets exist.
Compare identity rather than value, especially with duplicates.

title: Lowest common ancestor in a binary search tree
summary: Descend while both target values lie on the same side; otherwise the current node is the lowest branching point.

sections.heading: Meaning and boundaries
paragraphs: Input is a strict search tree, and p and q are actual nodes in it. Find their lowest common ancestor. Unlike an ordinary tree, value ordering lets each step rule out an entire side. Values are unique, so comparisons suffice for route selection; return the original node object. A target itself can be the common ancestor.

sections.heading: Core idea and invariant
paragraphs: If p and q are both smaller than the current value, both lie left, so the current node is not lowest and descent continues left. If both are larger, continue right. Otherwise they split across the sides or one equals the current value; the current node is the answer. These cases cover every value relationship.

sections.heading: Derivation and correctness
paragraphs: The loop invariant says the current subtree contains both targets. Descending their shared side preserves it. At a split, every descendant lies on just one side and cannot contain both, so the current node is lowest. If a target equals the current node, no strict descendant can be its ancestor, so stopping is also correct.

With target values 2 and 8 and current root 6, they split across the root, so return 6 without reaching either target. At current value 10, both lie left and descent continues. Sorting the targets only simplifies comparisons; the returned original root still preserves object identity and no replacement node is created.

sections.heading: Python implementation and adaptations
paragraphs: Iteration keeps only a root pointer and saves space compared with general postorder. Taking the smaller and larger target values can simplify comparisons, but do not assume p is smaller. The code can return None on some invalid inputs, but this is not complete missing-target validation. The proof still assumes the original problem's guarantees.

time: O(h).

walkthrough: Root 6 exceeds both targets; go left.
Current value 2 equals the smaller target.
Return node 2.

pitfalls: Global search-tree ordering is required.
Both targets are guaranteed to exist; this is not an existence validator.

title: Insert into a binary search tree
summary: Follow comparisons to an empty position, returning subtree roots and reattaching changed children.

sections.heading: Meaning and boundaries
paragraphs: Insert a new value into a strict search tree while preserving existing relationships and ordering constraints. The original problem guarantees the value is absent; the example additionally leaves the tree unchanged for duplicates. Inserting into an empty tree returns a new node. The caller must capture it or the new root will not be saved in the external variable.

sections.heading: Core idea and invariant
paragraphs: The recursive contract returns the current subtree root after insertion. At a null entry, create a node. Recurse left for a smaller value and right for a larger one, then assign the returned subtree to the corresponding child. The current root itself stays in place and is returned. Deletion and trimming reuse this return-and-reattach pattern.

sections.heading: Derivation and correctness
paragraphs: Every ancestor on the comparison path restricts the new value's range. Following the correct direction to an empty slot automatically satisfies all ancestor constraints; other subtrees stay unchanged. Reattaching every returned root prevents the new node created at a null child from being lost. Only one leaf position gains a node.

Inserting [1,2,3,4] successively forms a right chain, demonstrating that insertion preserves ordering but does not guarantee balance. Applications needing sustained query performance require rotations or another rebalancing mechanism. In a tree of existing height h, this algorithm visits at most one root-to-null-position path.

sections.heading: Python implementation and adaptations
paragraphs: Do not call solve(root.left,value) and ignore its return: a new node returned from a null entry must become its parent's child. In-place mutation changes the existing tree; returning root does not copy it. Duplicate support requires choosing left placement, right placement, or a count field. This example explicitly avoids adding duplicate nodes.

time: O(h).
space: O(h) recursion stack, with one new node.

walkthrough: 5 exceeds 4; go right.
5 is smaller than 7; go left.
Create 5 at the null entry and attach it as 7's left child.

pitfalls: The caller must capture a potentially new root.
Reattach recursive results from null children.

title: Delete a node from a binary search tree
summary: Handle zero, one, or two children; with two, copy the inorder successor's value and then delete that successor.

sections.heading: Meaning and boundaries
paragraphs: Delete a given value from a strict search tree and return the new root, preserving structure if the value is absent. Deleting the root or a one-child node changes the subtree entry, so reattach every recursive return. The task requires a valid search tree, without fixing one particular reconstructed shape.

sections.heading: Core idea and invariant
paragraphs: Locate the target by value. Without a left child, return the right; without a right, return the left. These rules include leaves. With two children, find the minimum in the right subtree, the inorder successor. Copy its value into the target position, then delete that successor from the right subtree so the value appears only once.

sections.heading: Derivation and correctness
paragraphs: The right subtree's minimum exceeds every original left-side value and is no greater than any other right-side value, so replacement preserves ordering. The successor has no left child, reducing its eventual deletion to a zero- or one-child case. Only the search path and successor path change; other subtrees retain their constraints.

Deleting a root with only a right child returns that child, changing the root object. Deleting a two-child root often keeps its object but changes its value. Both are numerically correct, yet identity differs. External node references therefore need care: deletion does not guarantee that an object continues to represent its original value.

sections.heading: Python implementation and adaptations
paragraphs: Copy the value, rather than assigning the successor reference directly to root, which would lose the target's child connections. root.right=solve(...) is essential or the original successor could remain. This implementation mutates stored node values. If node identity is bound to immutable records, choose a deletion strategy that moves nodes instead.

time: O(h); locating the target and successor takes a combined path length proportional to tree height.

walkthrough: Target 3 has two children.
The minimum node on its right is 4; copy 4 over value 3.
Delete the original leaf 4 and preserve left child 2.

pitfalls: After copying the value, delete the original successor.
Deleting the root can return a different node; capture that return.

title: Trim a binary search tree
summary: When a node is out of range, use ordering to discard an entire side and recurse only where valid values can remain.

sections.heading: Meaning and boundaries
paragraphs: Keep nodes in the closed interval [low,high], remove others, and preserve the relative structural relationships of retained nodes. Endpoint values are included. Unlike deleting one value, one trim can change many subtree entries or the whole root. low<=high and strict search-tree ordering are guaranteed.

sections.heading: Core idea and invariant
paragraphs: If the root is below low, every value on its left is smaller still. Discard both root and that side, returning only the trimmed right subtree. If root exceeds high, discard its oversized right side and retain the trimmed left. Keep an in-range root, trim both children, and reattach them.

sections.heading: Derivation and correctness
paragraphs: Discarding a whole side relies on global ordering and cannot lose a valid node. For a retained node, valid descendants are reattached through returned subtree entries, so removing intermediate nodes does not lose them. Each step removes invalid nodes or promotes original descendants to entries, without changing retained values.

For root 0 below range with valid right child 2, return 2 as the new entry rather than an empty tree, and continue trimming its descendants. An out-of-range node can still have a valid side, so do not discard its entire subtree immediately. Only discard a side whose complete invalidity follows from ordering.

sections.heading: Python implementation and adaptations
paragraphs: Use strict <low and >high for exclusion, not <= or >=. The returned root can be a deep descendant, so call root=solve(root,low,high). Python's references and garbage collection determine whether removed nodes are freed immediately. Algorithmic deletion here means disconnecting them from the output tree.

time: O(n) worst case; ordering may skip many nodes.

walkthrough: Root 3 is in range and stays.
Node 0 is too small; move to its right child 2.
Discard oversized 4 and keep 2's left child 1.

pitfalls: Both interval endpoints are included.
Whole-side pruning is invalid for an ordinary binary tree.

title: Convert a sorted array to a binary search tree
summary: Choose each interval's midpoint as root to keep child node counts close and construct a balanced search tree recursively.

sections.heading: Meaning and boundaries
paragraphs: Given a strictly increasing array, construct a height-balanced search tree. Different midpoint choices can yield different valid results; this example fixes the lower midpoint of a closed interval. An empty array returns None. Do not build directly in array level order: sorted order corresponds to a search tree's inorder, not its level order.

sections.heading: Core idea and invariant
paragraphs: Every element before the midpoint is smaller, and every element after it larger, so they can form the left and right subtrees. Let lo and hi bound the current interval and choose mid=(lo+hi)//2 as root. The child intervals differ in length by at most one. Repeated midpoint selection maintains this balance down to leaves.

sections.heading: Derivation and correctness
paragraphs: For every interval, the midpoint ensures search-tree ordering. Recursively building two nearly equal-length intervals yields heights differing by at most one and thus satisfies balance. Every array position becomes a root exactly once, without omission or duplication. Lower versus upper midpoint selects a valid shape without changing inorder.

An even-length interval has no unique midpoint. For [1,2], a lower midpoint gives root 1 with right child 2; an upper midpoint gives root 2 with left child 1. Both are balanced with the same inorder, so automated tests should not reject the alternative. This example fixes the lower midpoint for stable level-order display. Inorder equality and height balance should be the main correctness conditions.

sections.heading: Python implementation and adaptations
paragraphs: Pass indices rather than slices to avoid array copying and keep auxiliary space within balanced tree height. The new tree takes linear space, usually listed separately as output. Sequential insertion is not a balanced construction: strictly increasing input makes an ordinary insertion tree a long chain.

time: O(n).
space: O(log n) recursion stack, plus O(n) new tree.

walkthrough: Choose midpoint 0 as root.
Choose -10 for the left interval and 5 for the right.
The remaining -3 and 9 become right children.

pitfalls: Valid output structure is not unique.
For duplicate input, first define the search-tree duplicate policy.

title: Convert a binary search tree to a greater sum tree
summary: Accumulate in descending right-root-left order so each node receives the sum of all original values at least as large as its own.

sections.heading: Meaning and boundaries
paragraphs: The original problem gives a strict search tree. Replace each value with the sum of original tree values greater than or equal to it, changing values but preserving child connections. Compute from original values; never add an already accumulated new value as another original contribution. Result values generally no longer follow the original search-tree ordering direction.

sections.heading: Core idea and invariant
paragraphs: Reverse inorder visits the right subtree, root, then left, producing descending values. Maintain running as the sum of all original values already visited.
