Add the current original value first, then write running to the node. At this point, previously visited nodes are exactly those with greater original values.

sections.heading: Derivation and correctness
paragraphs: The maximum is visited first and includes only itself. Assuming earlier updates are correct, running still sums their original values. The current node is not yet modified, so adding it does not count the old prefix twice. After writing, this node is never added again; later left-side nodes still contribute their own original values, completing the induction.

Negative values work the same way. For original values [-3,-1,2], visit 2,-1,-3 and obtain new values 2,1,-2 respectively. The running sum need not grow. Correctness depends on the visited set containing every larger value, not on monotonic growth of the sum.

sections.heading: Python implementation and adaptations
paragraphs: Iterative reverse inorder mirrors the ordinary template with left and right exchanged. The add-before-assignment order is essential. Values here are distinct. With duplicates, per-node accumulation gives equal original values different results; group equal values and update them together instead of reusing this implementation directly.

time: O(n).

walkthrough: At 4, running is 8+7+6+5+4=30.
At 0, running is the whole-tree sum 36.

pitfalls: Add the current original value; do not count updated values again.
Duplicates require separate group handling.

title: Binary tree level-order traversal II
summary: Collect normal level order, then reverse level order while keeping each level left to right.

sections.heading: Meaning and boundaries
paragraphs: Return levels from deepest to root, still ordering each level left to right. Reverse order between levels, not order within a level. An empty tree returns an empty list. Normal [[1],[2,3]] becomes [[2,3],[1]], not [[3,2],[1]].

sections.heading: Core idea and invariant
paragraphs: BFS processes in its natural direction to collect all levels, then applies reverse to the outer list. Bottom-up output does not require searching for parents from leaves. Ordinary nodes usually lack parent references, so reverse expansion would need an extra index. Once boundaries are known, reversing the level list is enough.

sections.heading: Derivation and correctness
paragraphs: Normal level order places every node on the correct level and orders that level left to right. Reversing the outer list moves inner lists without changing their contents, preserving horizontal order. The deepest level moves from last to first and the root from first to last, giving the required reversed level order.

A chain has one node per level but up to n levels, making repeated front insertion and outer-list shifting particularly costly. Appending at the end followed by one reversal stays linear. The completed output merely rearranges levels: values are not recomputed and no tree child references change.

sections.heading: Python implementation and adaptations
paragraphs: answer.reverse() reverses the outer list in place without creating a second outer list. Repeated insert(0,level) can take O(h²) shifts across h levels and is no longer linear on chains. deque.appendleft also avoids that problem, but still needs final conversion to the required list.

time: O(n); reversing at most O(h) outer entries is bounded by O(n).

walkthrough: First obtain the three levels from root to leaves.
Reverse only the outer list.
The third level becomes the first answer item.

pitfalls: Do not reverse node order within levels.
List front insertion can be quadratic on deep trees.

title: Binary tree right-side view
summary: Take the last visited node of each level; deep nodes from the left subtree can also appear in the view.

sections.heading: Meaning and boundaries
paragraphs: Imagine viewing the tree from its right side. Return the rightmost visible value at each depth. Rightmost refers to horizontal position within a level, not the chain found by following right pointers. If the right subtree ends early, deeper left-subtree nodes can still appear. An empty tree returns an empty list.

sections.heading: Core idea and invariant
paragraphs: Use left-to-right BFS with a fixed size each round. The last node popped is that level's rightmost. Append its value only when the index is size-1, avoiding a full per-level value list. Other nodes must still be processed because their descendants can become the next level's rightmost nodes.

sections.heading: Derivation and correctness
paragraphs: The claim is immediate for the root level. Adding children in parent level order, left before right, maintains left-to-right order on the next level. Thus the round's last node is truly rightmost even when it belongs to the root's left subtree. Taking one per level produces h results ordered top to bottom.

If the root's right child is a leaf while its left child has a deeper right child, that grandchild also appears in the view. Visibility is compared independently at each depth, regardless of whether its ancestor appeared in the preceding view. Selecting each level's last node expresses this independence; searching only children of previously visible nodes would fail. Per-level selection directly implements the definition.

sections.heading: Python implementation and adaptations
paragraphs: Do not stop when a right pointer is null, or deeper left-side nodes will be missed. DFS can instead visit right before left and record the first node at each new depth, another expression of same-level priority. This BFS uses an index to identify the final item and records zero or negative values normally.

time: O(n).

walkthrough: The first level ends with 1.
The second level ends with 3.
Only left-side node 4 remains on the third level, and it is visible.

pitfalls: The right-side view is not the right-child chain.
Do not skip children of other nodes at the current level.

title: Average values of binary tree levels
summary: Divide each level's sum by its frozen node count, storing statistics instead of full level lists.

sections.heading: Meaning and boundaries
paragraphs: Output the arithmetic mean of all values at each level, from root to deepest level. A one-node level has that node's value as its mean, still represented as a float. An empty tree returns an empty list. Level sizes can differ greatly; dividing the whole-tree sum by the number of levels cannot replace separate statistics.

sections.heading: Core idea and invariant
paragraphs: At each BFS level, record size and add each popped value to total. At the end of the round, compute total/size. Newly enqueued children are excluded because only the fixed number of current nodes is popped. Reset total for each level instead of carrying earlier values. Child enqueue order does not affect the sum.

sections.heading: Derivation and correctness
paragraphs: size counts the actual nodes on this level, and total sums exactly those values, so their quotient is the defined mean. Missing children are not enqueued and never enter the denominator as zeros. Every nonempty level has size at least one, avoiding division by zero. The empty tree returns before the loop.

For a negative-valued level [-3,-4], the mean is -3.5; integer division gives -4, losing the fraction and exposing floor-rounding behavior. Dividing each level's sum by its own count also keeps the mean between its minimum and maximum. This mathematical property can help detect wrong denominators or level boundaries.

sections.heading: Python implementation and adaptations
paragraphs: Python / performs true division; // rounds a noninteger mean and is incorrect here. Integer total accumulates at arbitrary precision, but the resulting float still has ordinary rounding error, typically accepted within a judge's tolerance. Applications needing exact rationals can return numerator/denominator pairs or Fraction without changing traversal boundaries.

time: O(n).

walkthrough: The first level has sum 3 and count 1.
The second has sum 29 and count 2.
The third has sum 22 and count 2.

pitfalls: Use / rather than //.
Missing children do not contribute to the denominator.

title: Find the largest value in each tree row
summary: Maintain a separate maximum for each level, using an initial state that reserves no valid integer.

sections.heading: Meaning and boundaries
paragraphs: Return the maximum node value at each depth. All values may be negative, so the initial maximum cannot be fixed at zero. An empty tree has no rows and returns an empty list. A row means a level, not a root-to-leaf path; same-level children of different parents participate in the same maximum.

sections.heading: Core idea and invariant
paragraphs: Run BFS by level. Begin each round with best=None, assign the first node directly, and use max thereafter. No numeric lower bound assumption is needed. Pop exactly the current level's node count, append best for that round, and reset it for the next.

sections.heading: Derivation and correctness
paragraphs: After k nodes in the round, best equals their maximum. Initially empty, the first node establishes the invariant; each max preserves it. After size nodes, best is the whole-level maximum. Children wait until the next round, so a larger child value cannot affect the parent level.

For [-8,-6], the result must be -6 rather than a default zero. If another level contains zero, best=0 is a valid statistic and must not be mistaken for uninitialized merely because it is falsey. Separating state from value with is None is a reusable habit for integer statistics.

sections.heading: Python implementation and adaptations
paragraphs: best is None explicitly tests initialization. Avoid if not best, since zero is a valid maximum. Negative infinity is another possible sentinel, but None is more direct for unbounded integers. No full current-level value list is needed; apart from the queue, only constantly many temporary variables are used.

time: O(n).

walkthrough: The root-level maximum is 1.
The second level compares 3 and 2.
The third compares 5, 3, and 9, obtaining 9.

pitfalls: Do not initialize the maximum to zero.
Reset current-level statistics every round.

title: Populate next pointers in a perfect binary tree
summary: Use the guarantee of exactly two children per internal node to link siblings and adjacent children across parents.

sections.heading: Meaning and boundaries
paragraphs: In a perfect binary tree, each internal node has two children and all leaves have equal depth. Link every node to its right neighbor at the same level, setting the level-end next to null. This perfect-tree-specific constant-space method differs from problem 117's general dummy-chain approach. It does not apply when children can be missing.

sections.heading: Core idea and invariant
paragraphs: With the current level linked through next, traverse it directly. For each parent, set left.next to right, and right.next to the left child of the next parent, or null if none exists. This links both siblings under one parent and adjacent children under different parents.

sections.heading: Derivation and correctness
paragraphs: Set the root's next to null to establish the first level. Assuming parent-level links are correct, linking each parent's children creates a complete left-to-right chain on the next level. Perfect structure guarantees next.left exists and that if the first node has a left child, every node in that level has children. Move to the next level with head=head.left.

Among leaves 4,5,6,7, nodes 5 and 6 have different parents, making their link the key cross-parent check. Setting only left.next=right produces separate chains 4→5 and 6→7 instead of one complete level. Existing parent-level next links are a necessary prerequisite for connecting their children across parents.

sections.heading: Python implementation and adaptations
paragraphs: Only head and node scanning references are used, without queue or recursion. Leaves need no child-link work because the preceding round already set their next pointers. Clearing root.next first replaces any stale root pointer; upper levels overwrite every subsequent level's links. Do not transfer these existence assumptions to an ordinary tree.

time: O(n).

walkthrough: The root links 2→3.
Node 2 links 4→5 and crosses parents with 5→6.
Node 3 links 6→7, with 7.next=None.

pitfalls: This applies only to perfect binary trees.
Use node.next.left for cross-parent connections.

title: Maximum depth of an N-ary tree
summary: Generalize the maximum of two child heights to the maximum across all children.

sections.heading: Meaning and boundaries
paragraphs: An N-ary node's children is an ordered child list; it may have no children or many. Maximum depth counts nodes from root to farthest leaf: zero for an empty tree and one for a leaf. Child count is not depth: a root with hundreds of leaf children still has only two levels.

sections.heading: Core idea and invariant
paragraphs: The same helper idea returns subtree height. Recursively compute every child height, take their maximum, and add one for the current node. With no children, maximum child height must be zero. Python max accepts default=0 for an empty iterator, avoiding a separate leaf branch.

sections.heading: Derivation and correctness
paragraphs: Every root-to-leaf path enters some child after the root, so the tallest child determines longest path length. Correct recursive child heights followed by a maximum cover every route. Varying child counts do not affect the proof; a fixed two-way comparison simply becomes a finite-set comparison.

For a childless root, the generator is empty, max returns its default zero, and adding one gives leaf height one. With many children, recursion finishes their heights one by one rather than keeping all branches active simultaneously. Each recursive generator level retains constant state, so the longest call chain determines auxiliary space.

sections.heading: Python implementation and adaptations
paragraphs: The example defines a separate Node class, independent of TreeNode's left/right fields. A generator expression computes child heights individually without building a list. Every edge is traversed once. Call-stack space depends on longest path h; many children are not recursed into simultaneously, so width does not directly set stack depth.

time: O(n), where n is the N-ary node count.
space: O(h) recursion stack; no complete list of child heights is stored.

example.input: Node 1 has children 2 and 3; node 3 has child 4
walkthrough: Leaves 2 and 4 have height one.
Node 3 has maximum child height one and its own height two.
The root has maximum child height two and returns three.

pitfalls: max needs a default for an empty sequence.
The number of children is not node depth.

title: Traversal recap: processing time and pending state
summary: Decide when to process the node, then represent that timing with recursion, marked frames, or a level queue.

sections.heading: Meaning and boundaries
paragraphs: First distinguish how results are organized: a linear visit sequence, depth groups, or aggregated subtree information. Preorder places parents before children, inorder places roots between left and right, and postorder places parents after children. Level order uses depth as its primary key and is not a simple rewrite of the three depth-first orders.

sections.heading: Core idea and invariant
paragraphs: The recursive call stack implicitly records suspension points; an explicit stack must preserve nodes and stages itself. Preorder schedules pending left/right work, inorder retains ancestors along the left chain, and postorder can use marked state. Reversing a root-right-left value list gives a postorder sequence but does not automatically perform real-time processing that depends on child results.

sections.heading: Derivation and correctness
paragraphs: Choose a template from dependencies. Top-down DFS commonly passes intervals or remainders from parents to children. Postorder suits parents needing heights, balance, or target reports from children. Same-level statistics and connections suit BFS or existing next chains. A unified marked template explains order, while individual problems can use simpler specialized implementations.

To debug timing, inspect three events around a node: on entry, neither child has been processed; at between, the left side is complete; at leave, both sides are complete. An action reading a right-subtree result at between has a dependency-timing error even if final visit output seems plausible. Move it to leave.

sections.heading: Python implementation and adaptations
paragraphs: The following event trace records entry, the point between recursive returns, and exit. Filtering enter, between, or leave from the same recursive structure yields all three traversals. Empty trees produce no events; each actual node produces exactly three. This reveals where recursion pauses and resumes more clearly than final output alone, and helps debug processing-time errors.

time: O(n), with three events per node.
space: O(h) stack, plus O(n) event output.

example.output: enter gives [1,2,3]; between gives [2,1,3]; leave gives [2,3,1]
walkthrough: Record enter when the root is entered.
Record the root's between after the left subtree exits.
Record its leave after the right subtree exits.

pitfalls: Function invocation and node processing are different events.
Marked-stack push order must reverse logical execution order.
Level order must freeze the current boundary.

tests.expression: [v for event,v in solve(tree([1,2,3])) if event=='between']

title: Depth recap: maximum, minimum, balance, and complete trees
summary: Height combinations must respect valid paths, balance checks must cover every node, and structural shortcuts need explicit guarantees.

sections.heading: Meaning and boundaries
paragraphs: Maximum depth concerns the longest root-to-leaf path, minimum depth the nearest actual leaf, and balance the height difference at every node. All involve height or depth, but replacing max with min does not convert one into another. An empty subtree supplies zero maximum height but is not a valid minimum root-to-leaf route.

sections.heading: Core idea and invariant
paragraphs: Postorder heights suit bottom-up combination; BFS levels identify the nearest leaf from the top. Balance needs failure information alongside returned height to avoid recomputation. Return a height/Boolean pair or encode failure as -1: the pair is more explicit, while the sentinel is more concise.

sections.heading: Derivation and correctness
paragraphs: Counting complete trees is a structural shortcut, not an ordinary height formula. Equal boundary heights imply a perfect subtree because the last level is continuously filled from the left. The inference is invalid for arbitrary trees. Distinguish h from n in complexity: an ordinary tree can have h=n, a complete tree has logarithmic height, and BFS queue space depends on width w.

Combining statistics does not always require visiting portions that cannot change the conclusion. For balance alone, a sentinel can short-circuit immediately. If accurate maximum depth is also requested, imbalance cannot stop traversal. The return contract determines permissible optimizations more fundamentally than an existing template, and tests should cover the meaning of every returned component.

sections.heading: Python implementation and adaptations
paragraphs: The following single postorder computes maximum height, minimum leaf distance, and balance together. For a missing child, the minimum chooses the existing side; when both are missing it returns one. Balance checks both child flags and the current height difference. A combined return contract shows how statistics share traversal while requiring different combination rules.

time: O(n); each node combines a constant number of statistics.

walkthrough: Leaf 3 has both maximum and minimum distance 1.
A node with only a right child takes that side's minimum plus one.
The root's height difference is 2, so it is unbalanced.

pitfalls: A missing child cannot form a minimum path.
Root height difference alone cannot establish whole-tree balance.
O(log n) height needs structural guarantees.

title: Paths and construction recap: input state, output ownership, and interval boundaries
summary: Path searches maintain the route, while tree construction maintains unconsumed intervals; both require precise entry and return contracts.

sections.heading: Meaning and boundaries
paragraphs: Path problems often pass accumulated ancestor information to children: current route, target remainder, or depth. Construction passes an interval into recursion and reattaches a newly built subtree root. Both restrict the subproblem while descending, but return different things: search may return a Boolean or collect answers; construction must return a node entry.

sections.heading: Core idea and invariant
paragraphs: A shared path needs paired append and pop because sibling calls reuse a mutable object. An integer remainder computed as a new value needs no undo. Copy collected lists or create strings to prevent later backtracking from rewriting history. A construction cursor generally must keep advancing or retreating; it must not be restored between sibling branches.

sections.heading: Derivation and correctness
paragraphs: With preorder plus inorder, build left first; with backward postorder plus inorder, build right first. Boundaries and consumption order together determine which subtree owns the next item. A maximum binary tree can first be understood through recursive interval maxima, then optimized with a decreasing monotonic stack. Do not call all recursion backtracking: construction does not try and undo candidates.

Paths can be stored as immutable tuples, but constructing each still costs proportional to its length. Construction outputs node references; parents reattach new subtrees rather than path copies. Understanding ownership and return meaning prevents mistakenly applying search-style undo to construction cursors or node links.

sections.heading: Python implementation and adaptations
paragraphs: This template returns every root-to-leaf path and its sum, using path.copy() for independent output ownership. It helps verify problems 112 and 113: filtering sums by a target gives existence and all matching paths. Only one temporary route is stored, without copying every recursive prefix. Copies occur only when a leaf path is actually output.

time: O(n+L), where L is the total node count in output paths.
space: O(h) temporary state, plus O(L) output.

example.output: Path [1,2,5] sums to 8; path [1,3] sums to 4
walkthrough: Copy the left path at leaf 5.
After leaving the left side, shared path is restored to [1].
Collect the right path independently; earlier answers stay unchanged.

pitfalls: Undo mutable path changes; consumption cursors generally must not be restored.
Collect root-to-leaf paths only at leaves.
Slicing and list concatenation can hide extra copying costs.

title: Search-tree validation recap: interval constraints and inorder monotonicity
summary: Use global intervals for validation and inorder for adjacent differences, run frequencies, and accumulation; agree on duplicate rules first.

sections.heading: Meaning and boundaries
paragraphs: Search-tree properties apply to whole subtrees, not merely direct children. Two equivalent validation routes pass ancestor intervals downward or check globally strictly increasing inorder. Strict increase forbids duplicates. When duplicates are allowed, nondecreasing order alone may not express left-only or right-only placement rules; intervals additionally need endpoint-inclusion flags.

sections.heading: Core idea and invariant
paragraphs: Search and lowest-common-ancestor queries follow one route and depend on h. Minimum difference and modes scan full inorder and depend on n. Minimum difference tracks adjacent gaps; modes track equal-value run lengths. Greater-sum conversion uses reverse inorder to carry the sum of processed larger values to each node. They share ordering but require different state updates.

sections.heading: Derivation and correctness
paragraphs: Insertion, deletion, and trimming return changed subtree entries for parents to reattach; validation is read-only. Greater-sum conversion changes only values, yet generally destroys the original ordering, so original search logic cannot be applied to the new values. Establish whether comparisons refer to original or transformed values.

For a tree allowing duplicates only on the right, checking nondecreasing inorder misses duplicates on the left. Validation must match the precise definition. Replacing strict comparisons with nonstrict ones does not make a validator universal. Interval checking can express these finer directional rules through whether equality is permitted at endpoints.

sections.heading: Python implementation and adaptations
paragraphs: The following inorder validator retains only the predecessor and requires each current value to be strictly greater. previous=None means no first node has been visited; zero cannot be a placeholder. Return immediately on failure. Success means every left-subtree value precedes and is smaller than its root, while every right-subtree value follows and is larger, establishing the full strict search-tree condition.

time: O(n).

walkthrough: The inorder prefix is 1, 5, 3.
3 is not greater than predecessor 5.
The global decrease proves the tree is not a strict search tree.

pitfalls: Check duplicate policies separately for each problem.
Local parent-child comparisons cannot replace global constraints.
Do not query a transformed greater sum tree using the original search-tree property.

title: Binary tree review: choose algorithms from information flow
summary: Establish input guarantees, return contracts, and dependencies before selecting traversal order and state containers.

sections.heading: Meaning and boundaries
paragraphs: For a tree problem, first ask three questions: is a search-tree, complete-tree, or perfect-tree guarantee given; how is empty input handled; and does output consist of statistics, paths, or a modified root? Guarantees determine valid pruning, while output determines return types. Distinguish equal values from identical node objects. Lowest common ancestors and node links usually operate on actual references.

sections.heading: Core idea and invariant
paragraphs: Top-down information includes target remainder, legal interval, and current route. Bottom-up information includes height, balance flags, and target-location reports. Horizontal information includes per-level statistics and next links. Parameterized DFS suits the first, postorder combination the second, and BFS or scans along existing same-level chains suit horizontal tasks. Inorder's special power comes from search-tree ordering.

sections.heading: Derivation and correctness
paragraphs: Separate space for recursion or explicit stacks O(h), queues O(w), temporary paths O(h), and output. All-path output can exceed linear size. Reconstruction and merging allocate nodes, so list output-tree space. Time analysis must look beyond counting nodes: slicing, string concatenation, repeated height computation, and front insertion can hide quadratic work.

During review, write a one-sentence contract for every recursive helper: return current subtree height, return the trimmed entry, or decide whether the current interval permits all descendants. If the return cannot be explained clearly in one sentence, refine the design before coding. A clear contract also makes empty cases and parent combination rules easier to verify individually.

sections.heading: Python implementation and adaptations
paragraphs: The following level-based diagnostic counts nodes, height, and maximum width. It explains why equal-n trees can have different space behavior: chains have width one but large height, while wide trees have the opposite shape. Use these statistics to design tests after studying: empty trees, single nodes, long chains, negative values, missing children, extremely wide levels, and search-tree counterexamples with deep ancestor-constraint violations.

time: O(n).

walkthrough: Level sizes are 1, 2, and 4.
Accumulate node counts and increment height per level.
The largest level size gives width 4.

pitfalls: Do not treat every binary tree as a search tree or balanced tree.
After an operation returns a changed entry, save the new root.
Include output and implicit copying in complexity.
